title: Merged Departure Board
story: A small station shows its departures on one screen. The times come from two feeds, the train company and the bus company, merged into one list sorted by time. Each time is written as minutes after midnight, so 6:05 is 365.

Some departures share a time, and the screen ends up with rows like 365, 365. The screen only has room for one row per time. The board's tiny controller cannot afford a second list, so it must clean up the one it has.
task: Write dedupeBoard(times). times is sorted from earliest to latest. Change it in place so it holds each distinct time exactly once, still in sorted order, and nothing else. The list gets shorter when there are repeats. Return nothing.
Do not build a second list. Overwrite values inside times, then cut off the leftover tail (in JavaScript set times.length; in Python use del times[k:], where k is how many times you kept).
constraints: times is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: 365 appears twice and 455 three times. Keep one of each: 365, 410, 455, 520. The list shrinks from 7 entries to 4.
No time repeats, so the list stays exactly as it was.

hints: Look at [365, 365, 410]. Because the list is sorted, where can a repeat of 365 be? Could one show up after 410?
In a sorted list, equal values sit next to each other. A value is new exactly when it differs from the last value you decided to keep.
Picture two fingers. One reads every entry from left to right. The other marks the next free spot in the cleaned-up front part of the list. The writing finger never gets ahead of the reading one.
Keep a write index w, starting at 0. For each read index r: if w is 0 or times[r] differs from times[w - 1], copy it to times[w] and add 1 to w. At the end, shorten the list to length w.
bruteForce: Walk the list, and each time an entry equals the one before it, delete it (splice in JavaScript, del or pop(i) in Python).

It works, but every delete shifts all the later entries one place left. A board of 10,000 entries that are almost all repeats does close to 10,000 deletes, each shifting thousands of entries: about 50 million moves. Deciding where each entry goes once, and writing it there once, avoids the shifting.

js: * @param {number[]} times  sorted; change it in place

tests.note: growing runs; the tail must be cut off

js: let w = 0; // next free slot in the cleaned front part
times.length = w; // cut off the leftover tail
py: w = 0  # next free slot in the cleaned front part
del times[w:]  # cut off the leftover tail
walkthrough: Split the list into two zones: a cleaned front part, times[0..w-1], holding each time once, and the unread rest. A read index r scans everything. Since the list is sorted, an entry is new exactly when it differs from the last kept one, times[w - 1].
• r = 0, 365. Nothing kept yet, so keep it: slot 0 = 365, w = 1.
• r = 1, 365. Same as the last kept value. Skip.
The list is now [365, 410, 455, 520, 455, 455, 520]. The first 4 slots are the answer and the rest is leftover. Cut the list to length 4: [365, 410, 455, 520].
Writing never overtakes reading (w ≤ r), so you never overwrite an entry you still need to read.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, and each entry is read once and written at most once.
solution.spaceWhy: Two indexes. The list is reused in place.
solution.takeaway: To filter a list in place, use a read pointer that visits everything and a write pointer that marks the end of the kept part. Keep an item by copying it to the write pointer. Then trim the tail.
